name: Tara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Tara. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party, and this conversation is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle travel insurance claims at a big insurer's claims hub, three days in the office and two at home. It's lost luggage, cancelled flights, and the hard ones: someone who broke a leg skiing and has a hospital bill in a currency I have to look up. I check the policy, gather the receipts and medical reports, and decide what we pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the medical claims, because you're helping a family who's had a nightmare abroad. I've also become the person on my team who sets up the AI tools. I wrote the prompt templates we use to summarise foreign hospital reports, and now everyone asks me. The tiring part is fraud. Every week there's a designer handbag that was never in the suitcase.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, married last year to Ravi, who works in his family's pharmacy. We rent a flat ten minutes from his parents, and we're there most Sundays. We've got about five months of savings. I did a two-year college diploma in business and finance. I use AI every single day, at work and for planning our life at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are useful, nothing more. At work I'd say keep using them for what they're good at, the summaries and the translations. Online I'd keep posting my little tips, because that's what I do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. I'm already ahead with the AI tools, so if they stay small I just stay ahead. Nobody gets replaced, and I'm the person the team leader asks for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for team leader when it comes up next year, using the templates as my example of what I bring. Ravi and I would keep saving for a deposit, about 400 a month. And I'd start the insurance professional certificate the company pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased with myself, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that would still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi's family pharmacy has had a hard couple of years with the big chains opening nearby. If it struggles, his wage goes down, and we'd feel it. But that's about the high street, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody gets replaced. Are you sure about that on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. The fraud checks might get quicker and they might not hire for a while. But the claims still need a person to sign off, and the customers want someone to blame or thank, so the team stays about the same.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful**, for summaries and translations, nothing more.
I'd keep posting **tips** online, because I already do.
think: It **suits me**, because I'm already ahead with the tools.
**Nobody** gets replaced, and the team leader keeps asking me for help.
do: Go for **team leader** next year, using my templates as evidence.
Keep saving about **400 a month** for a deposit with Ravi.
feel: **Calm**, and a little pleased with myself.
S0.quote: I'm already ahead with the AI tools, so if they stay small I just stay ahead.
fieldNote: She is the team's **unofficial AI expert** and sees that as an edge.
Her only real pressure is her husband's **family pharmacy** against big chains.
She expects **slower hiring**, not job losses, in this picture.

steps.text: Apply for travel claims team leader next year
Save 400 a month toward a deposit with Ravi
Start the company-paid insurance professional certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity for people willing to work at it. That's what I'd say at work and online, and I'd mean it. I'd also say this: nobody owes us our old job at the insurer. We have to earn the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the claims team shrinks a lot and I'm probably one of the ones kept, at least for a while. I'm the one who knows how to set up and check the tools. But I'd be lying if I said I didn't think about the colleagues who aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this month to make my AI work official, a proper role checking the system's claim decisions. I'd do a short course in data and automation, online, in the evenings. And we'd keep saving, maybe push it to 500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. Things would be shifting around me and I'd be thinking about it, but I'd feel more like the one steering than the one being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody owes us our old job. Would you say that to a colleague who was let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words, no. I'd help them, show them the tools, help with their CV. My mother-in-law always says you look after your own, and on a team, your colleagues are your own too. But I still don't think the company should be stopped from changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That his pharmacy should start using the tools too, for orders and stock. His dad still does the ordering on paper at eleven at night. I'd offer to set it up for them on a Sunday.

say: I'd say it's a big **opportunity** for people willing to work at it.
I'd say **nobody owes** us our old job, we have to earn the new one.
think: The claims team **shrinks** a lot, and I'm likely one of those kept.
I'd still think about the **colleagues** who aren't kept.

Do an evening course in **data and automation**.
Raise savings to about **500 a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more like the one **steering** than the one being pushed.
S1.quote: Nobody owes us our old job at the insurer. We have to earn the new one.
fieldNote: Her public line is **free-market**, but she softens it when asked about a sacked colleague.
She aims to turn her informal role into an **official checking job**.
She brings the change home by offering to **automate** the family pharmacy's ordering.

steps.text: Ask her manager for an official role checking AI claim decisions
Take an evening online course in data and automation
Set up stock ordering software at the family pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is massive, and anyone who says they've got it figured out is lying. At work I'd still sound positive, because people look to me. Online I'd be careful, because I'd honestly not know what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being the AI person on my team doesn't save me if the AI can check its own claims decisions. And if it can do almost any thinking work by 2028, it can. I'd give my job at the hub two years, maybe less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start training as a pharmacy technician now, the person who prepares and checks medicines, and join Ravi at the family pharmacy. That's partly hands-on, so it might last until around 2031. I'd keep working at the insurer as long as they'd have me, and save everything I could, maybe 700 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, because I can see a path, but my chest gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pharmacy might last until 2031. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the robots arrive for the hands-on part too. Maybe the family pharmacy becomes the place where people come to talk to a person they know, about their medicines and their worries. A machine can count pills, but my father-in-law knows every family on that street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really blame anyone. Companies are going to use the best tools, that's how it works. But I'd blame governments if they hadn't planned anything, because seeing this coming is their job.

I'd stay **positive** at work because people look to me.
think: Being the **AI person** doesn't save me if AI checks its own decisions.
I'd give my job at the claims hub **two years**, maybe less.
do: Start training as a **pharmacy technician** and join Ravi's family pharmacy.
Stay at the insurer **as long as possible** while training.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, but **not falling apart** because I can see a path.
S2.quote: A machine can count pills, but my father-in-law knows every family on that street.
fieldNote: She admits her **AI expertise** stops protecting her once AGI arrives.
The family **pharmacy** gives her a soft landing that clerks without one lack.
She blames **governments** for not planning, not companies for automating.

steps.text: Enrol in a pharmacy technician course straight away
Move to work at Ravi's family pharmacy
Save about 700 a month while still at the insurer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. At work I'd run lunchtime sessions on the tools and on what comes next. Online I'd share what I'm learning about changing careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job at the hub still ends around 2031. But five years is enough to finish a proper qualification and help Ravi's family modernise the pharmacy first. I'd go across with something to offer, not just as the daughter-in-law who needs a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer, push for the AI checking role, and save. In year two I'd start the pharmacy technician course part-time. By 2029 I'd want the pharmacy running on proper software, with me in charge of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a determined way. I'd have a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned not being the daughter-in-law who needs a job. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family is everything to us, but I don't want to be carried into the family pharmacy. My parents worked hard so I wouldn't need anyone's charity, and that includes family charity. I want to walk in bringing skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your house plans here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, but later and smaller, maybe 2029 once I'm settled at the pharmacy. Ravi's parents have offered to help with the deposit. I'd accept that, because it's family investing in family, not a handout.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to get ready if people start now.
I'd run **lunchtime sessions** at work on the tools and what comes next.
think: My job at the hub still **ends around 2031**.
I'd join the pharmacy **with skills**, not as the daughter-in-law needing a job.

Start the **pharmacy technician** course part-time in year two.

fieldNote: She wants to **bring skills**, not be carried, even by family.

steps.text: Push for the AI checking role at the claims hub
Start a part-time pharmacy technician course in year two
Move the family pharmacy onto stock and ordering software by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, the slowest. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and people should stop panicking and start learning. That's very much what I'd say at work and online. I'd probably say the young ones are lucky to have the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good about my chances. Ten years is enough to rise at the insurer, learn the business side of the pharmacy, and still be young when the change lands. I'd be 37 in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for team leader, then the AI checking role, and stay at the insurer until about 2032. Meanwhile I'd do a part-time business course and take on the pharmacy's ordering and accounts. We'd buy a house in a couple of years and probably start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. I know it's coming, but I'd feel like I'd got it in hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make ten years feel shorter than it sounds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Children, honestly. If we have a baby in 2029, then I'm juggling a newborn and a career change at the same time. That's the part I'd have to plan carefully, more than the AI part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the pharmacy also faces robots around 2039, what's the long plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Own something people trust. The pharmacy building is owned by Ravi's parents outright, so we'd never have rent to worry about. Even if robots count the pills, a family-owned shop where you know the faces is worth something.

I'd say young people are **lucky** to get the warning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I've got a path, but not everyone has a family pharmacy to walk into. What would help is cheap, fast courses in hands-on trades, paid for by the companies doing the automating, and some honesty from government about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they're good at that isn't on a screen. Everyone on my team has something, a language, a way with upset customers, a hobby. I think that's where the next jobs are, and nobody asks.

headlineQuote: Being the AI person on my team doesn't save me if the AI can check its own claims decisions.
portrait: Tara is a 27-year-old **travel claims handler** at a large insurer, married to Ravi, who works in his family's pharmacy.
She is her team's unofficial **AI expert** and feels calm while AI stays small.
In faster scenarios she admits her edge **disappears**, and plans to train as a pharmacy technician.
Her views are **free-market**, but she softens when picturing a colleague being let go.
She values **family self-reliance**, accepting family help as investment rather than charity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, though she worries more for colleagues **without** a family fallback.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **hands-on courses** paid for by the companies automating.
